article_title: Typical learning for whom? Guidelines for selecting benchmarks to calculate months of learning
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, Melissa Diliberti, Andrew McEachin, Jon Schweig, Louis T. Mariano. (2023). Typical learning for whom? Guidelines for selecting benchmarks to calculate months of learning. Research brief. https://www.nwea.org
title: Select benchmarks for months-of-learning calculations deliberately, guided by the metric's trade-offs
description: The brief's central recommendation, reflected in its title, is that benchmarks of typical learning used to calculate months of learning should be selected deliberately, since the choice of benchmark shapes the resulting months-of-learning figure. The authors write to "inform future uses by researchers and media" and discuss "how to calculate this metric as well as its trade-offs". Because the metric has major downsides despite its accessibility, users should weigh those trade-offs when choosing benchmarks.
requirements: An explicit benchmark of typical learning must be chosen before translating test scores into months of learning
constraints: The translation has major downsides despite its perceived accessibility
target_learners: K-12 students whose achievement is reported in months of learning
target_learning_goals: Accurate communication of student achievement relative to typical learning
examples: The brief provides guidelines for selecting benchmarks to calculate months of learning, aimed at researchers and media
key_sources: Megan Kuhfeld, Melissa Diliberti, Andrew McEachin, Jon Schweig, Louis T. Mariano. (2023). Typical learning for whom? Guidelines for selecting benchmarks to calculate months of learning. Research brief. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/73510/

article_title: Understanding, Valuing, and Utilizing Skills-First Practices as an Organization Supporting Frontline Workers and Jobseekers
citation: Carter, B., & Jacobs, B. (2025, July). Understanding, valuing, and utilizing skills-first practices as an organization supporting frontline workers and jobseekers. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/256
title: Guiding principles and key elements framework for an aligned skills-first system
description: The report presents a framework of twelve guiding principles (e.g., worker-centricity, access to sustainable and inclusive skills-based pathways, transparency and trust) paired with eighteen key elements (e.g., skills mapping to outcome-oriented learning pathways, establishing a common skills language, leveraging technology for skill development and matching), organized into five categories from worker empowerment to data and continuous improvement. The report states organizations "can utilize these guiding principles and key elements as a framework" to assess programs, modify curriculum design, engage employers, and empower jobseekers to understand their own skills and navigate opportunities.
requirements: All key stakeholders (employers, workers, educators, community-based organizations, policymakers, training providers, researchers) are at the table to collaboratively design each aspect of the system
target_learners: frontline workers and jobseekers across frontline industries
target_learning_goals: skills mapping to outcome-oriented learning pathways; career pathway navigation; skills validation and transferable credentialing
examples: The framework pairs principles such as worker-centricity with elements such as incorporating jobseeker/worker voice from the beginning and prioritizing belonging in matching

article_title: Integrating AI-Enabled EdTech in PK16 Education: Five Recommendations
citation: Ruiz, P., Peters Hinton, V., Prado, Y., Noakes, S., Liberman, B., Chillmon, C., Van Nostrand, P., Shell, A., Karim, S., Dallas, D., & Zachariah, I. (2025). Integrating AI-enabled edtech in PK16 education: Five recommendations for state and district leaders. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/273
title: Set clear classroom guardrails and restrict high-risk AI applications such as automated grading
description: The brief recommends districts establish comprehensive governance frameworks defining appropriate AI use boundaries through co-designed policies involving educators, learners, and families. It specifies that "high-risk applications including those affecting student assessment, disciplinary decisions, or personal data should not rely solely on AI systems." Policies should be context-driven and flexible across differently resourced districts while maintaining strong safety standards.
requirements: Co-designed responsible use policies defining when AI tools are helpful and where human judgment is essential
Professional learning and safeguards embedded into procurement and adoption processes from the start
constraints: District capacity varies dramatically, from thousands of staff with dedicated tech teams to just a handful of employees
Studies highlight the importance of training teachers to adapt AI use to promote critical thinking and avoid learner overreliance on automated outputs
target_learners: PK16 students, including learners with disabilities and multilingual learners
target_learning_goals: Responsible, equitable, and critical use of AI-enabled classroom technologies
examples: The brief's Appendix 2 catalogs risks including biased facial recognition in test proctoring, AI-generated false content, and educator overdependence on algorithmic recommendations, and recommends a govern-map-measure-manage lifecycle approach

article_title: Design Principles for Schools: Putting the Science of Learning and Development into Action
citation: Learning Policy Institute & Turnaround for Children. (2021). Design principles for schools: Putting the science of learning and development into action. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/
title: Guiding Principles for Equitable Whole Child Design framework
description: The report presents an organizing framework, the Guiding Principles for Equitable Whole Child Design, comprising five elements: positive developmental relationships, environments filled with safety and belonging, rich learning experiences and knowledge development, development of skills habits and mindsets, and integrated support systems. It states that "The organizing framework to guide transformation of learning settings for children and adolescents is reflected in the five elements shown in Figure 1.1". Each element is linked to research from developmental and learning science and to structures and practices for changing conditions, adult practice, and student learning. The framework aims at healthy development, learning, and thriving that is transformative, culturally affirming, empowering, and personalized.
requirements: Implementation across classroom, school, district, and larger macrosystem levels, joined together to produce an intentionally integrated developmental enterprise
constraints: The report notes the elements "have not yet been widely used to develop and create learning settings, nor have they been engineered in fully integrated ways"
target_learners: k-12 students
target_learning_goals: deep understanding and application of content
empathetic and ethical contribution to community

constraints: The report presents the framework as a synthesis of research syntheses, not as a tested model in this study

target_learning_goals: whole child development including academic, social, emotional, and physical well-being

article_title: GIFT-AI: Teaching the Game and Leveling the Field: Peer and AI Review + Reflection in a Business Writing Course
citation: MacArthur M, Minnillo S, Sperber L, Whithaus C and Stillman N (2025) GIFT-AI: teaching the game and leveling the field: Peer and AI Review + Reflection in a business writing course. Front. Commun. 10:1615752. https://doi.org/10.3389/fcomm.2025.1615752
title: Offer guided introduction to AI literacy in writing courses to level the playing field for underprepared and multilingual students
description: Because students enter writing courses with different academic preparation, English fluency, and prior AI experience, the authors argue that a guided introduction to AI literacy is an equity measure. They cite evidence that underprepared students appear less likely to use AI and more likely to misuse it, and that students with educated parents tend to be more likely to use chatbots, concluding that "Offering a guided introduction to AI literacy in Business Writing can therefore level the playing field for all students." The PAIRR model operationalizes this by positioning AI neither as a tool to correct deficient writing nor as a way to avoid writing, but as an additional supportive perspective that does not replace human feedback.
requirements: Course-level clarity on acceptable and unacceptable AI uses
Instructor willingness to address AI misuse through supportive conversation and rewrite options rather than plagiarism reports
constraints: Rationale rests partly on cited prior studies rather than on data collected in this article
target_learners: underprepared students
first-generation, low-income, and multilingual writers
examples: When Haoyu over-relied on AI for the first assignment, the instructor spoke with him in office hours about the value of his voice and unique experience, and he rewrote the assignment for a new grade

article_title: Guarded adoption of generative AI in higher education: high-achieving students, successful-student identity
citation: Jason Zagami. (2026). Guarded adoption of generative AI in higher education: high-achieving students, successful-student identity, and epistemic agency in a single-university mixed-methods survey. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education 23:47. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00625-6
title: Guarded adoption: selective, bounded, verification-intensive AI use in defence of epistemic control and successful-student identity
description: Guarded adoption is the paper's proposed interpretation of how high-achieving students relate to generative AI: "a form of selective engagement in which students use AI, but under conditions that seek to preserve epistemic control, intellectual ownership, and the legitimacy of their own learning". It is explicitly not scepticism, technophobia, or refusal; the concern is whether AI "remains subordinate to the learner's judgment". The article offers it as one plausible interpretation of the observed achievement-patterned differences, not a validated construct or general theory of student identity under AI conditions.
requirements: Requires attending to the conditions under which students accept AI use, not just adoption counts or enthusiasm ratings
constraints: The article states it is one plausible interpretation, not a general theory of student identity under artificial intelligence conditions; successful-student identity is used as an integrative analytical label, not an established or previously validated construct
target_learners: higher education students, particularly high-achieving students (self-reported GPA bands of 5.5 or above)
target_learning_goals: maintaining epistemic agency and independent judgment while using generative AI for learning
examples: A student who uses AI as a tutor-like conversational aid "but only while 'confirming accuracy'"; a student who lets AI assist with collecting and organising material but insists synthesis remains "solely my own"

Guarded adoption of generative AI in higher education: high-achieving students, successful-student identity, and epistemic agency in a single-university mixed-methods survey. article_title: Beyond Access: Guided LLM Scaffolding for Independent Learning in Undergraduate Statistics
citation: Mohammad Amanlou, Yasaman Amou-Jafari, Fereshte Bagheri, Fatemeh Boloukazari, Mehrad Liviyan, Elahe Khodaverdi Nadrabadi, Shahab Sherafat, Behnam Bahrak. (2026). Beyond Access: Guided LLM Scaffolding for Independent Learning in Undergraduate Statistics. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Computers in Education. https://github.com/MohammadAmanlou/Guided-LLM-Scaffolding
title: Six-family guided LLM-use protocol operationalizing scaffolding, help-seeking, self-regulation, and AI-literacy principles
description: The guided-use protocol is a student-facing training and rule set delivered before Topic 2 with weekly reminders, framing the model as "a fallible tutor rather than an answer source" and emphasizing "explanation-seeking, stepwise help , verification, and ethical use." It defines six observable rule families: R1 process-over-answer, R2 concept tutoring, R3 stepwise-hint seeking, R4 active practice and retrieval, R5 verification and calibrated trust, and R6 ethical/no-help use. The authors describe it as translating established learning-science principles into transcript-codeable LLM-use behaviors rather than a generic prompting template.
requirements: Explicit slide-based orientation with examples of productive and unproductive prompts before LLM use begins, plus weekly reminders
constraints: The same LLM platform and model were used in both LLM-access conditions; guidance differed through training and rules rather than a separate model or hard-coded guided mode
target_learners: second-semester Electrical Engineering and Computer Engineering undergraduates
target_learning_goals: probabilistic reasoning including conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, random variables, and distributions
examples: Three raters independently coded 67 student-practice transcripts against the six rule families, reaching Fleiss' κ = .896 before consensus

article_title: A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies
citation: Hingle, A., & Johri, A. (2025). A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies. https://www.google.com/search?q=A+Guided+Inquiry+Approach+to+Students+Co-Designing+Generative+AI+Course+Policies
title: Conceptual model positioning students as co-designers of course policies through guided inquiry, perspectival thinking, and student voice
description: The article's conceptual model (Figure 1) positions students not only as learners but as co-designers of course structures and policies. It integrates guided inquiry as the activity frame with perspectival thinking from situated learning theory and principles of student voice, so that "perspectival thinking, informed by situated learning theory and principles of student voice, helps students examine AI policy guidelines from multiple stakeholder perspectives." The model treats the GenAI policy itself as both an artifact for student engagement and a pedagogical tool, complementing top-down policy analyses by centering student agency.
requirements: A guided inquiry learning environment with curated resources and structured individual-then-collaborative policy design tasks
Instructor and institutional support for multi-stakeholder discussion
constraints: The study reframes policy as a social process rather than a fixed institutional document; co-design does not imply instructors or students alone bear responsibility for policy development
target_learners: undergraduate students in technology ethics coursework
examples: Students completed readings, used GenAI to brainstorm policy ideas, wrote individual policies with at least five justified elements, then collaborated in groups of 4-6 for roughly 45 minutes to craft a collective policy

article_title: From tool to scaffold: Structured human–AI collaboration and its effects on academic writing and digital critical thinking
citation: Alshehri OAO, Lamouchi A, Abdellatif MS, Al-Dosari MNA, Mekheimer M and Nemt-allah MA (2026). From tool to scaffold: structured human–AI collaboration and its effects on academic writing and digital critical thinking among Saudi EFL learners. Front. Psychol. 17:1830103. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1830103
title: Guided human–AI collaboration workflow with five components and AI-use logging
description: An instructional component in which the experimental group received "explicit instruction in a guided human–AI collaboration workflow built around five interrelated components": problem framing and prompt design; generating alternative outlines, arguments, and claims; iterative drafting and revision; verification and triangulation of claims and citations; and responsible-use regulation. Students used a generative AI assistant for idea development and structural scaffolding alongside a language-feedback tool, and each major assignment included an AI-use log documenting prompts, outputs consulted, and accept/reject decisions with justifications.

Explicit instruction in the five workflow components
An AI-use log per major assignment documenting prompts, outputs, and accept/reject/justify decisions

Without structured workflows and accountability mechanisms, risks of over-reliance and superficial learning are substantially elevated

target_learning_goals: Digital critical thinking and AI literacy
examples: Over 11 weeks, students progressed from prompt-design training through three guided writing assignments with AI-use logs, verification training using Google Scholar and institutional databases, and responsible-use instruction

article_title: Examining Variation in How Guided AI Tutors Resolve Student Impasses
citation: Ahtisham, B., Vanacore, K., Napoli, A., Arens, J., Ionova, K., Cohn, C., Salehi, S., & Kizilcec, R. (2026). Examining Variation in How Guided AI Tutors Resolve Student Impasses. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38346
title: Guided AI Tutor: a guardrailed LLM chemistry tutor with a scripted problem-solving planning protocol
description: The Guided AI Tutor is an LLM-based tutor (GPT-4o via the OpenAI API) that guides students to plan solutions to multistep chemistry problems without giving them the solution. Its behavior is controlled entirely by a prompt covering a role as a problem-solving coach, objectives, behavioral guidelines (never solve the problem, ask one question at a time, give "increasingly specific, targeted hints" after incorrect answers), a problem with four scripted questions, and response-handling rules. Its planning sequence is organized around eight problem-solving practices.
requirements: A detailed prompt protocol specifying role, objectives, behavioral guidelines, scripted questions with reference answers, and response-handling rules
constraints: Escalation after errors is requested only as a natural-language instruction; the article found the tutor sometimes continued questioning after earlier questioning failed
target_learners: undergraduate students in an introductory general chemistry course at a large research university
target_learning_goals: planning solutions to multistep chemistry problems following expert problem-solving practices
examples: Students used the tutor through a stand-alone web application to plan solutions to 8 assigned chemistry problems, producing 1,260 sessions and 20,462 student turns

article_title: Evaluating Prompt Injection Defenses for Educational LLM Tutors: Security-Usability-Latency Trade-offs
citation: Alexandre Cristovão Maiorano. (2026). Evaluating Prompt Injection Defenses for Educational LLM Tutors: Security-Usability-Latency Trade-offs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06669
title: Select educational AI guardrails as explicit trade-offs among bypass resistance, false-positive behavior, and latency
description: The article argues that "guardrail choices in educational AI should be made as explicit trade-offs among bypass resistance, false-positive behavior, and latency, rather than from isolated metrics." Because false positives carry direct pedagogical cost in tutoring systems, the optimal operating point depends on institutional risk and usability requirements: NeMo's balanced rail blocks all attacks but frustrates roughly 1 in 6 students, while the multi-layer pipeline preserves usability at higher residual bypass.
requirements: Institutional tolerance for false positives and latency must be specified before selecting a guardrail configuration
constraints: The article does not claim absolute security; a 46.34% input-gate bypass indicates significant residual risk, and latency figures are hardware-dependent
target_learners: students in educational AI tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: preserving pedagogical integrity and productive struggle while maintaining access to legitimate help
examples: The sensitivity sweep (Table 9) shows three configurations reaching 0% FPR that differ by orders of magnitude in latency and monetary cost rather than usability

citation: Keith Tran, Samiha Marwan, and Thomas Price. (2026). Teaching Prompt-Based Programming with LLMs: A 45-Minute Lesson with Guided Practice for End-User Programmers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30547
title: Gulf of Envisioning framework as a design lens for prompting instruction
description: The article adopts the Gulf of Envisioning framework (Subramonyam et al.) to explain why learners may fail even when using powerful AI tools, and uses it to organize its intervention. "By scaffolding learners' ability to describe the problem (capability), phrase prompts effectively (instruction), and assess output quality (intentionality), we aim to reduce the cognitive gap between intent and implementation." The lesson's five learning objectives are aligned with the framework's three gaps, framing prompt-based programming as a learnable CS-specific skill.
requirements: Instruction and practice addressing each of the three dimensions: capability, instruction, and intentionality
constraints: Applied in this article to prompt-based programming tasks where learners specify computational intent in natural language
target_learners: end-user programmers
novices using LLMs for programming
target_learning_goals: expressing computational intent clearly to LLMs
examples: The lesson mapped specifying function structure to the instructional gap, describing data transformation to the capability gap, and debugging failed prompts to the intentionality gap

article_title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
citation: Bastani Hamsa, Bastani Osbert, Sungu Alp, Ge Haosen, Kabakcı Özge, Mariman Rei. (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. description: The article's central design recommendation: generative AI tools "must be deployed with appropriate guardrails when learning is important." article_title: Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
citation: Alfieri, L., Brooks, P. J., Aldrich, N. J., & Tenenbaum, H. R. (2011). Does Discovery-Based Instruction Enhance Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(1), 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021017
title: Provide feedback, worked examples, scaffolding, and elicited explanations rather than unassisted discovery
description: The article concludes that "unassisted discovery does not benefit learners, whereas feedback, worked examples, scaffolding, and elicited explanations do." Designers of discovery-based instruction should embed guidance — regular feedback, provided solutions, scaffolded support, or prompts to self-explain — because enhanced discovery outperformed other instruction (d = 0.30) while unassisted discovery underperformed explicit teaching (d = -0.38).
requirements: Discovery tasks must include a guidance mechanism (feedback, worked examples, scaffolding, or elicited explanation) to produce the enhanced-discovery advantage
constraints: Pure, unassisted discovery-learning practices lack evidence of improving learning outcomes and should be abandoned, per the article's reading of Mayer (2004)
target_learners: children
adolescents
adults
target_learning_goals: acquisition of concepts, strategies, and problem-solving skills across academic domains
examples: The enhanced-discovery meta-analysis coded generation, elicited explanation, and guided discovery conditions, which together yielded d = 0.30 over comparison instruction

article_title: Meta-Analysis of Inquiry-Based Learning: Effects of Guidance
citation: Lazonder, A. W., & Harmsen, R. (2016). Meta-analysis of inquiry-based learning: Effects of guidance. Review of Educational Research, 86(3), 681-718. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315627366
title: Six-type typology of inquiry learning guidance ordered by specificity
description: The meta-analysis adopts T. De Jong and Lazonder's (2014) framework, which "organized their framework according to the specificity of the guidance learners need to successfully perform an inquiry." It orders six types from least to most specific: process constraints, status overviews, prompts, heuristics, scaffolds, and explanations. Process constraints "give no overt directions at all but instead organize the inquiry into a series of manageable subtasks"; prompts "remind the learner to perform a particular action"; scaffolds assist "by explaining what to do and how to do it"; explanations "offer the most specific type of guidance." Each type is matched to an intended audience in Table 1, from learners with matured inquiry skills to learners largely incognizant of the action.
requirements: Guidance must be classified by its specificity (extensiveness/explicitness) rather than by the inquiry phase or skill it supports, so that differential effects across age groups can be tested
constraints: Category labels reflect the meta-analysis's terminology and "do not necessarily match the designation used in the original study"; scaffolding fading is often absent in short-term inquiries because inquiry skills develop slowly
target_learners: Learners aged 5 to 22 in math and science education, from children to adolescents
target_learning_goals: Scientific reasoning skills: generating hypotheses, designing experiments, evaluating evidence, and acquiring domain knowledge through inquiry
examples: The Go-Lab environment incorporates scaffolds assisting elementary, middle school, and high school learners in formulating research questions, generating hypotheses, and designing experiments

article_title: A Unilateral Grading Contract to Improve Learning and Teaching
citation: Danielewicz, Jane and Peter Elbow. (2009). A Unilateral Grading Contract to Improve Learning and Teaching. College Composition and Communication 61(2). https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.14394/23309
title: Guarantee a grade for completing specified activities so teacher and student attention shifts from grading to learning
description: The article's core design recommendation: specify in writing the activities that reliably produce good writing, and promise the base grade for completing them regardless of judged quality. The stated aim is that "teachers and students give as much attention as possible to writing and as little as possible to grades." Evaluation continues throughout the semester, but it is decoupled from the base grade, so feedback stops functioning as a grade signal and students keep control over concrete activities they can fulfill.
requirements: The contract must list activities the teacher has found reliable in producing the target quality of work over the term
All decisions about what is acceptable for the base grade must be made without regard to judgments of work quality
constraints: Institutional settings that require final grades force hybridity; the authors would not use grades at all outside such institutions
Students desperate for grades higher than the base grade remain in hock to teacher evaluation
target_learners: first-year college writing students
honors students
basic writers
students alienated from writing
target_learning_goals: sustained effort, revision, and participation in writing processes
examples: Jane and Peter use essentially the same ten-provision contract in their first-year writing courses, guaranteeing a B for attendance, meeting due dates, participation, informal writing, peer feedback, substantive revision, copyediting, conferences, and portfolio submission

article_title: A preliminary examination of gut microbiota, sleep, and cognitive flexibility in healthy older adults
citation: Anderson Jason R., Carroll Ian, Azcarate-Peril M. Andrea, Rochette Amber D., Heinberg Leslie J., Peat Christine, Steffen Kristine, Manderino Lisa M., Mitchell James, Gunstad John. (2017). A preliminary examination of gut microbiota, sleep, and cognitive flexibility in healthy older adults. Sleep Medicine, 38, 104-107. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7433257/
title: Altered gut microbiome composition as a possible mechanism linking inadequate sleep to poor neurocognitive outcomes in older adults
description: The article proposes that dysbiosis of the gut microbiome may contribute to cognitive dysfunction associated with chronically poor sleep, framing "altered gut microbiome composition as a possible mechanism linking inadequate sleep to poor neurocognitive outcomes." The account draws on animal-model work showing diet-driven microbiome changes can reduce cognitive flexibility and on human work showing partial sleep restriction alters microbiome composition. The authors position this as a hypothesis requiring prospective and experimental confirmation, not a tested mechanism.
requirements: Prospective and experimental studies to confirm the proposed mediational relationship
constraints: The observational nature of the preliminary study precludes causal conclusions
Cross-sectional assessments can distort mediational relationships
Possible mechanisms such as systemic inflammation were not examined

examples: The study measured gut microbiome composition via 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of stool samples and correlated phylum proportions with PSQI scores and Stroop subtest performance

article_title: A Randomized Control Study of Instructional Approaches for Struggling Adult Readers
citation: Greenberg Daphne, Wise Justin, Morris Robin, Fredrick Laura, Nanda Alice O., Pae Hye-K. (2011). A randomized control study of instructional approaches for struggling adult readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3237050/
title: Guided repeated oral reading fluency component with 40% words-per-minute improvement target
description: Three conditions (DF, DCF, DCEF) included a fluency component using a guided repeated oral reading approach. Each participant received a passage at his or her instructional level from Timed Readings Plus or Jamestown Fluency Readers, read it aloud to establish a baseline of correct words per minute, and was given a stopwatch to practice independently for 15 minutes. The target was for learners "to independently practice a passage until they improve their correct words read per minute of that passage by 40% over baseline." Upon meeting or exceeding the target rate, participants moved to a new passage with a new baseline.
requirements: Passages at instructional level, a stopwatch, independent practice time of 15 minutes, and teacher verification of the target rate
target_learners: Struggling adult readers in adult literacy programs
examples: Time allocations included 15 minutes of fluency practice in the DF, DCF, and DCEF conditions

citation: Cremers, P. H. M., Wals, A. E. J., Wesselink, R., & Mulder, M. (2016). Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9398-5
title: Guidebook for Hybrid Learning Configurations
description: A written document reifying the set of design principles as a boundary object. Its final version contained three chapters: an introduction defining HLCs and their rationale; the design principles with a short description of the Value in the Valley HLC; and the context description with each principle's features, their effects, and conditions for those effects. Participants used it as preparation, common prior knowledge, and "a reference book when developing the HLC".

constraints: Some participants expected an instruction guide with a working method and found practical application vague; a respondent suggested adding examples beyond Value in the Valley

target_learning_goals: understanding and applying research-based design principles when designing or evaluating an HLC
examples: A feature of fostering authenticity—working on an authentic assignment—was reported to motivate students, conditional on a client being actively interested in the results

article_title: The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic
citation: Tessa Eysink, Sanne Dijkstra, Jan Kuper. (2002). The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016018210897
title: Guidance and manipulation as complementary instructional variables in computer-based problem solving
description: The article proposes that two instructional variables play complementary roles in computer-based problem solving for concept development. Guidance leads students to see all situations relevant for developing new knowledge, benefiting performance directly after instruction; manipulation leads students to play around so that they systematically experience the results of their actions through feedback, benefiting retention. The authors state that "guidance in combination with the possibility to manipulate objects in a domain, support the acquisition of knowledge and skills in that domain".
requirements: Guidance must expose learners to all different types of basic problem situations derivable from the target concept
Manipulation requires a visual representation with objects whose manipulation yields feedback on the results of actions
constraints: Evidence concerns learning the conditional in first-order logic with social science students in Tarski's World
target_learners: first- and second-year social science students
target_learning_goals: problem-solving knowledge and skills in a domain
examples: In the experiment, guidance was operationalised via problems covering all basic problem situations, and manipulation via a manipulable visual representation

article_title: Scientific reasoning abilities in kindergarten: dynamic assessment of the control of variables strategy
citation: Joep van der Graaf, Eliane Segers, Ludo Verhoeven. (2015). Scientific reasoning abilities in kindergarten: dynamic assessment of the control of variables strategy. Instr Sci 43:381–400. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9344-y
title: Expose kindergartners to guided hands-on multivariable experiments to prepare them for later science education
description: The article recommends that young children be given hands-on, multivariable experiments with guidance from a teacher or other students, within their zone of proximal development, before they can perform such experiments independently. It argues that because the dynamic assessment task showed children "capable of correctly designing multivariable experiments with up to four variables manipulated at times", kindergartners should be exposed to such tasks, which prepare them for later science education based on experiments with multiple variables.
requirements: Sufficient guidance from a teacher or other students, consistent with the zone of proximal development
Hands-on materials in which multiple variables can be manipulated and compared across two setups
constraints: The supporting evidence comes from an individual dynamic assessment session in a quiet place in one school, not from classroom practice; the sample was small and the authors call for replication
target_learners: kindergartners aged 4 to 6 years
target_learning_goals: designing unconfounded multivariable experiments (control of variables strategy)
preparation for later experiment-based science education
examples: In the study, children designed hands-on experiments with two ramps, starting with one variable to set and progressing to four, with feedback after each experiment

article_title: Sociocultural Contexts and Relationships as the Cornerstones of Students’ Motivation: Commentary on the Special Issue on the “Other Half of the Story”
citation: Guay, F. (2022). Sociocultural Contexts and Relationships as the Cornerstones of Students' Motivation: Commentary on the Special Issue on the "Other Half of the Story". Educational Psychology Review, 34, 2043–2060. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09711-3
title: A four-element commentary framework for the development of academic motivation
description: In his commentary on the special issue on the "Other Half of the Story" of academic motivation, Guay organizes the discussion around four elements he enumerates explicitly: "the challenges of integrating central motivational constructs", "interpersonal relationships as supports for motivation at school", "school or cultural contexts that sustain motivation", and "new avenues for research". The framework positions sociocultural contexts and relationships as cornerstones of students' motivation, and is intended to stimulate research that advances the field while being useful to professionals working day to day with children and adolescents.
requirements: The framework is a commentary structure over the special issue's articles on the development of academic motivation and interpersonal relationships
constraints: It is a commentary, not an empirical test; the article text available is the abstract-level framing
target_learners: children and adolescents in school
examples: The commentary discusses the special issue's articles under the four enumerated elements rather than as isolated studies

article_title: Guided activity kits impact parents’ scaffolding of child STEM play
citation: Karen L. Bierman, Lynn S. Liben, Meg Small, Jennifer Connell, Brenda Heinrichs, Jessica Menold, Scarlett Rae Miller, Morgan Mannweiler. (2025). Guided activity kits impact parents’ scaffolding of child STEM play. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102082
title: Guided STEM activity kits with embedded stories, parent tips, and extension ideas
description: Guided activity kits are self-guiding material kits for parent-child play containing materials for building wooden structures plus guidance features. By random assignment, "kits were either “guided” (included embedded stories, parent tips, and extension ideas; n = 50) or “basic” (identical construction activities without guidance features; n = 25)." The guidance features are the manipulated component tested for increasing parents' STEM talk during play.
requirements: Kits must pair construction materials with embedded stories, parent tips, and extension ideas, as the guided condition did
constraints: The comparison basic kits contained identical construction activities without guidance features
target_learners: preschool children (Mage = 4.82 years) and their parents
target_learning_goals: STEM vocabulary and scientific inquiry talk during parent-child play
examples: Families received five activity kits containing materials for building wooden structures over 10 weeks, with guided kits adding embedded stories, parent tips, and extension ideas

article_title: Role-playing monument exploration: an online educational game with a role-playing mechanism and multi-dimensional scaffolding for monument tours
citation: Shu-Wei Liu, Hung-Yu Chan, & Huei-Tse Hou. (2025). Role-playing monument exploration: an online educational game with a role-playing mechanism and multi-dimensional scaffolding for monument tours. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10480-3
title: Guides role-playing historical characters as dynamic scaffolds within an authentic game context
description: A reusable design pattern in which instructors take on in-character roles (commander, soldier, invaders) inside an authentic virtual environment and deliver scaffolding dynamically according to the game situation. The article states that "the guides who role-played the soldier and commander could interact with learners according to the game situation and provide dynamic scaffolding to help learners solve task problems immediately", combining cognitive, procedural, emotional, and strategic support in character. This keeps support contextualized and immediate rather than delivered as out-of-character instruction.
requirements: Instructors able to stay in role and observe learner performance in real time
A game situation that calls for different scaffold types at different moments
constraints: The authors note it was a challenge whether instructors could provide the same level of scaffolding at different times, and the cost of guiding manpower
target_learners: adult learners in online game-based guide activities
examples: Soldiers gave knowledge hints and task procedures depending on learner performance; the commander checked submitted plans and gave strategic guidance; invaders appeared periodically to add uncertainty and require alertness

article_title: Insights on identifying potential types of guidance for supporting student inquiry when using virtual and remote labs in science
citation: Gamor, K.I. (2021). Insights on identifying potential types of guidance for supporting student inquiry when using virtual and remote labs in science. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09928-5
title: Taxonomy of guidance types for supporting student inquiry in virtual and remote labs
description: The article engages with a taxonomy of potential types of guidance for supporting student inquiry when using virtual and remote labs in science, drawn from the Zacharia et al. (2015) literature review it responds to. The article's keyword list names the guidance types covered: "Process constraints", "Performance dashboard", "Prompts", "Heuristics", "Scaffolds", "Direct presentation of information", "Automated guidance", "Automated tutoring", and "Adaptive feedback". The framework describes how and when to apply these guidance types across inquiry phases for optimal effect.
requirements: Guidance must be matched to the relevant phase of inquiry to achieve optimal effect, per the reviewed framework
target_learners: students conducting science inquiry with virtual and remote labs
target_learning_goals: science inquiry skills supported by guidance in computer-supported inquiry learning environments
examples: The article indexes the taxonomy's guidance types as keywords: process constraints, performance dashboards, prompts, heuristics, scaffolds, direct presentation of information, automated guidance, automated tutoring, and adaptive feedback.

citation: Larwin, K. H., & Larwin, D. A. (2013). The Impact of Guided Notes on Post-Secondary Student Achievement: A Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Teaching and Learning in Higher Education, 25(1), 47-58. http://www.isetl.org/ijtlhe/
title: Use guided notes as a low-cost, low-tech means of increasing engagement and achievement in lecture-based post-secondary courses
description: Guided notes are "teacher-prepared handouts that 'guide' a student through a lecture with standard cues and prepared space in which to write key facts, concepts, and/or relationships". The article recommends them as a "low-tech" inclusion that can significantly impact post-secondary achievement, based on its meta-analytic finding of a moderate overall effect. They are provided as handouts, electronically, or as PowerPoint slides with prompts and blank space.
requirements: Provided during lecture as an alternative to no notes, full lecture notes, or student-generated notes
Studies must use cues with prepared space for students to complete key content
constraints: Negative effects were found in single studies from mathematics and dentistry
All available research included undergraduate students only; no graduate-level studies were available
target_learners: post-secondary undergraduate students
examples: The meta-analysis included 12 studies across psychology, physics, mathematics, education, and dentistry, calculating 27 independent effect sizes from 1,529 participants

citation: Winter Lone, Neubauer Ricarda, Weimer Johannes, Dietrich Christoph F., Wittek Agnes, Schiestl Lina, Marinova Milka, Schäfer Valentin Sebastian, Strizek Brigitte, Recker Florian. (2024). Peer teachers as ultrasound instructors? – a systematic literature review of peer teaching concepts in undergraduate ultrasound education. title: Develop comprehensive guidelines for peer tutor education to standardize training and ensure minimum standards
description: The review concludes that despite growing literature supporting peer teaching in ultrasound education, training concepts remain heterogeneous without a standardized system for training and qualifying peer teachers. It recommends that "Developing comprehensive guidelines for peer tutor education could increase acceptance and recognition of peer-assisted learning and ensure minimum training standards." This addresses the observed variability in formats, durations, assessments and certification across programs.

constraints: The review is limited to undergraduate medical ultrasound education in English or German literature up to November 21, 2023, excluding postgraduate settings

medical students training as peer teachers
examples: Included programs used course-based concepts (93.8%) and internships (50.0%) with a median training duration of about ten days, with objective assessments such as MCQ or OSCE in 56% of programs

citation: Heyne, T., & Bogner, F. X. (2012). Guided Learning at Workstations about Drug Prevention with Low Achievers in Science Education. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v2n6p1
title: Guided learning at workstations: cooperative station work followed by group recapitulation, student-formulated questions, and researcher feedback
description: A modified open-learning pattern in which small groups work through self-instructional station materials at their own pace, then recapitulate what they learned with the researcher, formulate two questions arising from the group work, and receive feedback that closes knowledge gaps. Feedback should show students "what was achieved and what should or could have been achieved".
requirements: A pre-lesson ensuring a common basis of knowledge before station work
Specifically adapted learning materials matched to the low achievers' proficiency level
Separated phases of teacher intervention providing specific support after station work

title: Guided inquiry teaching method (GITM)
description: GITM is described as "a teaching method that enables students to acquire knowledge on their own under the tutelage of a teacher". requirements: A teacher who chooses the concept and guides students through investigation of it
target_learners: Secondary school physics students

examples: In this study the experimental group was taught light and sound waves with GITM for the treatment period while the control group received the conventional method

citation: Deke, J., Wei, T., Kautz, T. (2017). Asymdystopia: The threat of small biases in evaluations of education interventions that need to be powered to detect small impacts. (NCEE 2018–4002). title: Researchers powering evaluations to detect small impacts should guard against, avoid, or mitigate small biases rather than treating them as ignorable
description: The article's central design recommendation is that "biases that might have once been reasonably ignorable can pose a real threat in evaluations that are powered to detect small impacts". constraints: The article states its findings should not be interpreted as suggesting researchers should avoid powering evaluations to detect small impacts

examples: The report derives reduced attrition tolerances (Table 2), computes the parameter assumptions needed to retain standard bounds (Table 3), and benchmarks feasibility against 869 past WWC-rated RCTs (Table 6)

article_title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Tools for Online Database Instruction
citation: Mery, Y., DeFrain, E., Kline, E., & Sult, L. (2014). Evaluating the Effectiveness of Tools for Online Database Instruction. Communications in Information Literacy, 8(1). https://journals.lib.pdx.edu/index.php/informationliteracy
title: Interactive guided live-database tutorial pattern with linear steps and hands-on activities

examples: The study's GotS tutorial taught Academic Search Complete around the research question about social networking sites and romantic relationships, with ten listed learning objectives.

article_title: Implementation of Structured Inquiry Based Model Learning toward Students' Understanding of Geometry
citation: Salim, K. & Tiawa, D.H. (2015). Implementation of Structured Inquiry Based Model Learning Toward Students' Understanding of Geometry. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(1), 75-83. http://www.ijres.net

description: The article argues that because geometry concepts are abstract and students differ in cognitive ability, "a formula, a concept or principle in the geometry of space, should be rediscovered by students under the guidance of teachers (guided reinvention)". Teacher guidance structures the search so students rediscover the target concepts
constraints: The article notes conventional assumptions that knowledge transfers intact from teacher to student mind are a cause of learning difficulties in geometry
target_learners: high school mathematics students with varied cognitive abilities
examples: The experimental class learned geometry of space through hypothesis formulation, experiments on the learning material, and drawing conclusions under guidance

article_title: Using Rubrics as an Instructional Tool in EFL Writing Courses

constraints: The analysis sessions were conducted in students' mother tongue; the treatment covered two essay types over four weeks in one preparatory program
target_learners: university EFL preparatory-program students aged 18-20
target_learning_goals: internalizing criteria of good writing and applying them in compare-and-contrast and cause-and-effect essays
examples: In week 3 students scored a sample compare-and-contrast essay and justified their assigned scores with peers elaborating on justifications, without teacher interference

citation: Margunayasa, I G., Dantes, N., Marhaeni, A.A.I.N., & Suastra, I W. (2019). The Effect of Guided Inquiry Learning and Cognitive Style on Science Learning Achievement. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 737-750. https://www.e-iji.net
title: Guided inquiry learning model via Liewelyin's six-stage inquiry cycle
description: The article implements guided inquiry as a six-stage inquiry cycle from Liewelyin (2002): "(1) Inquisition - starting from the statement to be investigated, (2) Acquisition - enabling a brainstorming procedure, (3) Supposition - identifying the statement to be tested, (4) Implementation - designing and carrying out  a plan, (5) Summation - collecting evidence and drawing conclusions, and (6) Exhibition - sharing and communicating results." It was delivered over 12 meetings to fifth-grade science classes, with the teacher acting as facilitator rather than transmitting knowledge directly.
requirements: Students lack prior inquiry experience, so the guided format with teacher-posed questions and structured stages is used
Assessment during inquiry is continuous, using observation sheets, portfolio, and report product assessment
constraints: The article reports the model favored reflective-style students; impulsive students showed no significant advantage over conventional teaching
target_learners: fifth-grade elementary school students
target_learning_goals: scientific process skills such as predicting, experimenting, concluding, and communicating
examples: The experimental group experienced guided inquiry in 12 meetings across four elementary schools (SDN 1 Penarukan, SDN 4 Banyuning, SDN 1 Banjar Jawa, SDN 1 Baktiseraga)

article_title: The Impact of Peer Observation and Feedback on Technical Seminar Presentations: A Constructive Model
citation: V. Vijaya Vani. (2015). The Impact of Peer Observation and Feedback on Technical Seminar Presentations: A Constructive Model. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 5, No. 3, July-September. https://www.teachingenglish.org.uk/article/peer-observation
title: Give students guidance on what to observe before peer feedback so feedback is constructive rather than vague and negative
description: The article recommends structuring peer observation: before students observe peers' presentations, they should be given a format specifying the components to focus on, so their feedback is constructive rather than personal, vague and negative. The author states that "A structured format is generated to help peer observation group for providing feedback" and to make them aware of aspects of presentation skills to consider. Without such guidance, first-spell feedback generated confusion and highlighted negatives.
requirements: A structured format listing observable presentation parameters must be provided to observers before they give feedback
constraints: Derived from one small study of engineering students' seminar presentations; the article gives no test of the format's effect beyond participants' views
target_learners: tertiary students acting as peer observers of seminar presentations
target_learning_goals: giving constructive feedback and improving technical seminar presentation skills
examples: After the unguided first spell produced vague, negative comments, the author introduced a seven-parameter rating format for the second spell and discussed the resulting feedback with all participants

article_title: The Effect of Written Corrective Feedback on Grammatical Accuracy of EFL Students: An Improvement over Previous Unfocused Designs
citation: Mobin Khanlarzadeh, Majid Nemati. (2016). The effect of written corrective feedback on grammatical accuracy of EFL students: An improvement over previous unfocused designs. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research 4(2). https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Unfocused WCF design that aligns delayed-posttest errors with revised-task errors via guided tasks, repeated tasks, and elementary-level scope
description: This design pattern addresses the validity critique that unfocused WCF studies cannot ensure delayed-posttest errors match those targeted during revision. It uses guided writing tasks drawn from the learners' textbook, multiple writing tasks with revisions so errors are addressed repeatedly, and an elementary proficiency level where the range of grammar used is narrow. As the article states, "the writing tasks were guided and the topics were chosen based on the learners' textbook which required them to use certain grammatical structures."
requirements: Writing tasks must be guided and tied to grammatical structures learners are studying
Multiple writing tasks with revisions so learner errors are addressed many times
Feedback limited to grammar rules already studied or being studied during the semester
constraints: Findings apply to elementary-level learners who use a narrow range of grammar
target_learners: elementary EFL students
examples: Over three months, students completed a pretest, three guided writing tasks with revisions, and a posttest describing a famous person, with dominant structures intended to be the same across assignments.
key_sources: Mobin Khanlarzadeh, Majid Nemati. (2016). The effect of written corrective feedback on grammatical accuracy of EFL students: An improvement over previous unfocused designs. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research 4(2). https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr

article_title: Learning Solar System Using PhET Simulation to Improve Students' Understanding and Motivation
citation: Prima, E. C., Putri, A. R., & Rustaman, N. (2018). Learning Solar System using PhET Simulation to Improve Students' Understanding and Motivation. Journal of Science Learning, 1(2), 60-70. https://jurnal.uns.ac.id/science-learning
title: Guided worksheet with group discussion during PhET simulation activities
description: The experimental lessons paired the PhET simulation with a structured student worksheet in three parts (planet characteristics, orbit/gravity problems, and Solar System exercises) solved in groups of four or five. "Students solved th e questions in the worksheet in-group discussion during performing laboratory activity", and students could change gravity variables to see planetary movement, then concluded from group discussion. The teacher guided students and reviewed material in class using the same simulation.
requirements: A prepared worksheet whose problems are designed for analysis with the simulation; group organization; teacher guidance during activities
constraints: Worksheet exercises in the final part were completed in class without using PhET simulation
target_learners: 8th-grade junior high school students working in groups of four or five
target_learning_goals: Analyzing planetary motion, orbits, and gravity concepts
examples: Part A used planet-description cards shared between groups; Part B posed four orbit questions solved while operating the simulation in the computer lab

article_title: Use of Video Feedback in the Training of Pre-Service Teachers
citation: Andrews, A., Bobo, L., & Spurlock, A. (2011). Use of video feedback in the training of pre-service teachers. Journal of Instructional Pedagogies. (no URL printed in the article text)
title: Train pre-service clinical educators with guided video review of their own teaching rather than a teaching workshop alone
description: The article's central design recommendation is that training clinical educators should include viewing videotapes of one's own teaching followed by guided analysis with a researcher, because "the utilization of videotape feedback can assist in improving the amount of feedback provided by clinical educators". In the study, only the group that both attended the seminar and reviewed its recordings with guided feedback increased feedback frequency. A focused workshop on effective teaching skills alone could not improve feedback frequency as a stand-alone intervention.
requirements: Access to videotaped teaching sessions and a guided review period after each session, as Group One received 25 minutes after each teaching session to view and analyze recordings with the researcher
constraints: The article states further research is needed and that efficacy of videotape feedback in training pre-service teachers still needs to be researched; a workshop alone is insufficient
target_learners: pre-service clinical educators in health professions, here upper-class athletic training students
target_learning_goals: increasing the frequency and quality of augmented feedback given to students during clinical skills instruction
examples: Thirty pre-service teachers were randomly assigned to seminar-plus-video, seminar-only, or control groups and videotaped weekly for eight weeks while teaching taping and wrapping skills

article_title: A Study of the Relationship between Type of Dictionary Used and Lexical Proficiency in Writings of Iranian EFL Students
citation: Vahdany, F., Abdollahzadeh, M., Gholami, S., & Ghanipoor, M. (2014). A Study of the Relationship between Type of Dictionary Used and Lexical Proficiency in Writings of Iranian EFL Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.6p.31
title: Teachers should familiarize students with dictionary types and guide them toward appropriate dictionaries to improve lexical proficiency
description: The article recommends that EFL teachers make dictionary distinctions explicit and steer learners to suitable dictionary types. It states "By suggesting an appropriate dictionary type, teachers can help their students to improve their lexical proficiency as effectively as possible and enhance their EFL writing." This follows from the finding that dictionary type and skill relate to lexical proficiency.
requirements: Teachers must know learners' dictionary use habits, preferences, and the difficulties learners experience with different dictionary types
constraints: Findings come from upper-intermediate Iranian TOEFL learners; the authors call for replication with elementary and intermediate learners
target_learners: upper-intermediate Iranian EFL learners
examples: The study surveyed 80 learners' preferences and found bilingual (E-P) desk dictionaries most used, informing which dictionary types teachers should suggest

article_title: Convincing Science Teachers for Inquiry-Based Instruction: Guskey's Staff Development Model Revisited
citation: Zambak, V. S., Alston, D. M., Marshall, J. C., & Tyminski, A. M. (2017). Convincing Science Teachers for Inquiry-Based Instruction: Guskey's Staff Development Model Revisited. Science Educator, 25(2), 108-116. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1143566
title: Guskey's (2002) model of teacher change, adapted for this study's IBI-focused PD
description: Guskey's staff development model (2002) describes PD as an attempt to change teachers' instructional practices, to develop beliefs and attitudes towards different teaching approaches, and to improve students' learning outcomes. The traditional teacher change model suggests that a change in teacher beliefs and attitudes precedes a change in classroom practice. Guskey (2002) alternatively proposed a different model where changes in teachers' instructional practices and student achievement precede changes in psychological factors (e.g., beliefs). Because of the components emphasized in the PD (e.g., inquiry-based instructional practices, teacher beliefs, and student achievement), the authors developed an adapted version of Guskey's teacher change model to align with their goals.
requirements: The model requires measurement of teachers' instructional practices, beliefs, and student achievement to test the relationships among its components.
constraints: The study's data could not show evidence supporting the entirety of Guskey's model (2002).
target_learners: in-service middle school science teachers
examples: The study used a non-random, single group, interrupted time-series, quasi-experimental design to test Guskey's model of staff development.
key_sources: Zambak, V. S., Alston, D. M., Marshall, J. C., & Tyminski, A. M. (2017). Convincing Science Teachers for Inquiry-Based Instruction: Guskey's Staff Development Model Revisited. Science Educator, 25(2), 108-116. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1132092

article_title: Assessment of knowledge and awareness of cardiopulmonary resuscitation and heart attack symptoms amongst medical students in Syria - a cross-sectional study.
citation: Taghi Ali, Atia Mohammad, Mohaisen Mais Alreem, Al-Noufi Bushra, Sibai Mohamad, Nouh Sara, Arfeh Yaman, Alhamid Ahmad Abdul Hakim, Taghi Olya, Kheder Karam, Mahfouz Fawaz Ali. (2026). Assessment of knowledge and awareness of cardiopulmonary resuscitation and heart attack symptoms amongst medical students in Syria - a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08800-z
title: Guideline-mapped 11-item CPR knowledge score and 18-item MI symptom knowledge score instrument
description: The study's questionnaire adapts a previously validated instrument (used with the original authors' permission) and aligns knowledge items with 2020 American Heart Association resuscitation guidance, translated from English to Arabic and reviewed by bilingual investigators. CPR knowledge is scored as "an 11-item, guideline-mapped subset with unambiguous correct answers (score range 0–11)" and MI symptom knowledge as an 18-item score (range 0–18), each item scored 1 for correct and 0 for incorrect or 'not sure'. Internal consistency was Cronbach's alpha = 0.65 (CPR) and 0.58 (MI); the instrument was pilot-tested for usability (n = 10) and clarity/length (n = 12).
requirements: Requires sign-in-restricted online administration to limit duplicate submissions, as used in this survey
constraints: The authors report modest internal consistency (α = 0.65 for CPR, α = 0.58 for MI) and note the instrument measures theoretical knowledge only, without practical assessment
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: Assessing guideline-mapped CPR knowledge and MI symptom recognition for needs assessment and curriculum prioritisation
examples: Administered online via Google Forms to 500 students across nine Syrian medical schools between 13 and 30 June 2025, with 97.8% of submitted surveys fully completed and eligible for analysis.

article_title: "It turns out I was wrong": a thematic analysis of medical students' reflective writing in an e-learning course on communication skills.
citation: Janssen, L., Schick, K., Pittroff, S. I. D., Reiser, S., Bauer, J., Berberat, P. O., Gartmeier, M. (2025). “It turns out I was wrong”: a thematic analysis of medical students’ reflective writing in an e-learning course on communication skills. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08172-w
title: Steer reflective writing in e-learning with guided prompts covering awareness, understanding, and transfer
description: The article recommends that reflective writing in e-learning be steered by written guidelines and open questions targeting the three core elements of reflection: awareness, understanding, and transfer. “Students provided with writing prompts use more metacognitive strategies compared to those without prompts”, and repeated reflective writing across modules is said to enhance metacognitive awareness and reduce resistance to reflection.
requirements: Prompts kept broad so students can express thoughts without being overly constrained
Multiple reflective writing occasions across the course rather than a single sample
constraints: Explicit questions about emotional responses were excluded in this study to test whether students would reflect on emotions independently
target_learners: medical students learning online autonomously
examples: The course embedded three prompts at the end of each of three modules, yielding nine reflections per student

article_title: Effect of mental imagery using cognitive aids on the performance of novice anesthesiology residents during a simulated cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
citation: Levy Manon, Dopff Cécile, Audibert Gerard, Bouquet Antoine, Gurda Thomas, Sy Mohammed, Bleuze Pauline, Michelet Daphné. (2025). Effect of mental imagery using cognitive aids on the performance of novice anesthesiology residents during a simulated cardiopulmonary resuscitation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07782-8
title: Structure mental imagery training of a cognitive aid as relaxation before, guided imagery, and refocusing after, repeated at gradually increasing intervals
description: The article operationalizes mental imagery training for resuscitation following the meta-analytic recommendations of Goble et al.: "5 min of relaxation before the mental imagery session and 5 min of refocusing after the mental imagery session", with guided imagery based on an animated cognitive aid. Residents repeated the imagery autonomously after reminders on seven days with an interval that gradually increased in duration, and the last repetition fell one and a half months before the final assessment. The authors note there is no consensus on the number of repetitions or the optimal interval.
requirements: An initial training session introducing the cognitive aids, a guided imagery session with relaxation before and refocusing after, and reminders for autonomous repetition over the retention period.
constraints: There is no consensus on the number of repetitions or on the optimal interval between repetitions; the article chose 7 repetitions and notes optimal models for intervals and repetition numbers for long-term retention still need to be developed.
target_learners: first-year anesthesia residents
novice clinicians training for emergency situations
target_learning_goals: non-technical skills in critical situations such as communication, leadership, situational awareness, decision-making and teamwork
examples: Residents underwent a 5-minute 'cardiac coherence' relaxation, a guided mental imagery exercise using the SFAR cognitive aids based on an animated PowerPoint, 10 minutes of eyes-closed repetition, and a 5-minute relaxation session, then 7 reminders on days 2, 5, 9, 20, 36, 62 and 136.

article_title: The teaching dilemma of health education teachers in China and path exploration: a cross-sectional study of Guangdong Province.
citation: Wang Zhen, Zhu Lin. (2025). The teaching dilemma of health education teachers in China and path exploration: a cross-sectional study of Guangdong Province. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1607420
title: Self-made three-section questionnaire surveying health education teachers' basic information, teaching situation, and school-level conditions
description: A self-made questionnaire (Supplementary File 1) administered anonymously online to teachers in 232 primary and secondary schools in Guangdong. It comprised three sections: "basic information of teachers", "teaching situation, such as teaching grade and the degree of teaching difficulty", and "school level investigation" covering uniform teaching materials, teaching standards, evaluation criteria, and school value for health education. The teaching difficulty outcome was recorded on five levels and merged into easy versus difficult categories for analysis.
requirements: Participants currently engaged in frontline teaching work who volunteered; health education teachers identified by reporting undertaking or participating in health education teaching in the last academic year
constraints: The assessment of teaching difficulty remained inherently subjective, relying on self-reported evaluations without objective validation metrics; survey schools were selected by the local Education Bureau, which may have introduced selection bias
target_learners: Frontline primary and secondary school teachers in Guangdong Province
target_learning_goals: Measuring teaching difficulty and its influencing factors in school-based health education
examples: 5,416 questionnaires were collected, 5,291 were valid (97.69% effective rate), and 2,342 respondents (44.26%) were health education teachers
key_sources: Wang Zhen, Zhu Lin. (2025). The teaching dilemma of health education teachers in China and path exploration: a cross-sectional study of Guangdong Province. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1607420

article_title: Capability to identify and manage critical conditions: effects of an interprofessional training intervention.
citation: Santesson Ia, Schell Carl Otto, Bjurling-Sjöberg Petronella. (2024). Capability to identify and manage critical conditions: effects of an interprofessional training intervention. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05567-z
title: Twelve guiding principles for interprofessional simulation-based education (Ju et al.)
description: The article presents, citing Ju et al., twelve distilled guiding principles for interprofessional simulation-based education based on evidence-based guidelines. The principles cover equitable distribution across professions, active learning, interprofessional competency-based learning objectives and assessment, psychological safety, repeated and distributed practice, attention to differences and hierarchy, feedback during debriefing, sociological fidelity, program evaluation, facilitator training, and institutional support. The authors suggest these are "plausibly are also relevant for training in healthcare organizations" and use them to interpret why low, uneven coverage limited workplace-level effects.
requirements: Institutional policies supporting educators and health workers, including financial support, adequate time allocations, and adequate space and facilities
constraints: In times of staff constraints, implementing extensive training interventions is a challenge, leading to goal conflicts for decision makers
target_learners: interprofessional healthcare teams in training organizations
examples: The article's Table 8 lists all twelve principles with descriptions, e.g. equitable distribution: planning, implementation and learning done jointly involving all relevant professions

article_title: Educational achievement and bullying: The mediating role of psychological difficulties.
citation: Murphy, D., Leonard, S. J., Taylor, L. K., & Santos, F. H. (2022). Educational achievement and bullying: The mediating role of psychological difficulties. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 92, 1487–1501. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12511
title: Growing Up in Ireland Cohort'98 three-wave dataset with bullying item, SDQ, and Junior Certificate composite scores
description: The Growing Up in Ireland national longitudinal study child cohort (Cohort'98) supplied the data: waves at 9 years (N = 8568), 13 years (N = 7527), and 17 years (N = 6216), with 8214 children answering the bullying item. Bullying was a yes/no self-report; psychological difficulties used the 25-item Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire ("total difficulties score ranges from 0 to 40"); achievement used Junior Certificate grades converted to a 0–10 composite score per Table 1.
requirements: Analyses used full-information maximum likelihood in Mplus 7 to handle missing data, and the bullying question asked whether anyone "picked on you" in the past year.
constraints: The article notes it "is not possible to ascertain if the child is describing school‐based bullying or bullying by another influential person in the child's life", and no objective resilience measures existed in the dataset.
target_learners: Irish 9- to 17-year-old school students
target_learning_goals: Measuring bullying exposure, psychological difficulties, and mathematics and literacy examination attainment
examples: Attrition analysis showed dropouts differed on literacy, mathematics, income and mother's education from those remaining at all three waves.

article_title: The effects of training managers on management competencies to improve their management practices and work engagement of their subordinates: A single group pre- and post-test study.
citation: Adachi H, Sekiya Y, Imamura K, Watanabe K, Kawakami N. (2020). The effects of training managers on management competencies to improve their management practices and work engagement of their subordinates: A single group pre‐ and post‐test study. J Occup Health. https://doi.org/10.1002/1348-9585.12085
title: A guide to management for healthy vibrant workplace: a 150-minute manager training workshop with five sections
description: An original training program developed by a clinical psychologist and a professor of occupational mental health based on the HSE management competencies framework. It was "offered in the form of a 150‐min workshop comprised lectures on various topics, group works, and homework", delivered to 20-30 participants per session across four sessions by the same instructor. Its five sections are self-check with the SMCIT, announcing strengths, group discussion, presentation, and setting personal goals with action plans.
requirements: Participants are managers who supervise at least one subordinate worker; managers with management experience of <3 months were excluded
constraints: Delivered in a single finance company in Japan without a control group; the authors note it may not have been intense enough for effects lasting to 1-year follow-up
target_learners: Workplace managers in a finance company
target_learning_goals: Assessing own management competencies, gaining ideas about management behaviors through group discussion, and improving everyday management behaviors via personal goals and action plans
examples: Participants completed the SMCIT to self-assess strengths and weaknesses, announced their best-scored strength, discussed and chose three important management skills in small groups, and set personal goals with action plans

The effects of training managers on management competencies to improve their management practices and work engagement of their subordinates: A single group pre‐ and post‐test study.
